bracket: [Textbook misprint: the book prints the four option labels as (A), (B), (C), (C) — the fourth is labelled (C), duplicating the third, and no option is labelled (D). The options are relabelled (A)-(D) here in the printed order, so the option shown as (D) is the one the book prints last. Only the labels are affected; the four expressions are transcribed exactly as printed.]

[Textbook misprint: option (B) is printed as "It will move along a curved path, bending towards positive \(x\) axis". As printed, no option is correct — a particle already travelling along the positive \(x\) axis cannot bend towards it — while the derivation above gives a deflection towards the positive \(y\) axis. Read alongside option (C), which names the negative \(y\) axis, option (B) is a misprint for "positive \(y\) axis", and it is keyed here on that reading. The book prints no MCQ key anywhere, so this is an adjudication of the printed options rather than a disagreement with a printed key.]
[Textbook misprint: option (A) is printed as "remain uncharged". The intended word is "unchanged" — the particle's charge is not in question, its kinetic energy is.]
[Textbook misprint: the question ends "What must be the magnetic of \(B\)?". The intended word is "magnitude".]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key reads "3.0 cm, 18.7 MHz, 2.53 keV", and all three values disagree with the question's own data. From \(v = 3.2\times10^{7}\) m/s, \(B = 6.00\times10^{-4}\) T, \(m = 9.1\times10^{-31}\) kg and \(e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\) C the correct values are \(r = 30.3\) cm, \(f = 16.8\) MHz and \(KE = 2.91\) keV. The printed set is also inconsistent with ITSELF: a radius of 3.0 cm at 18.7 MHz implies \(v = 2\pi r f = 3.52\times10^{6}\) m/s and hence a kinetic energy of 0.035 keV, not the 2.53 keV printed beside it. No single choice of the constants reproduces all three printed values.]

[Textbook misprint: the question supplies "charge of electron \(= 1.62\times10^{-19}\) C". The accepted value is \(1.60\times10^{-19}\) C, and the book's own printed answer of \(6.643\times10^{-27}\) kg follows from 1.60 and not from 1.62 — the latter would give \(6.72\times10^{-27}\) kg. The working above therefore uses \(1.60\times10^{-19}\) C, which also returns the accepted alpha-particle mass. The stem separately prints "a transverse a uniform magnetic field", with one article too many.]
[Textbook misprint: the question reads "in apposite directions". The intended word is "opposite", which is what the book's own printed answer of "Repulsive" requires.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key is \(8.355\times10^{-5}\) T. From \(I = 5.2\) A at \(d = 3.1\) cm, \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d} = \dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times 5.2}{0.031} = 3.355\times10^{-5}\) T. Every digit after the first agrees with the correct value, so the printed key differs from it only in its leading digit — 8 where 3 belongs.]

[Textbook misprint: the question reads "the force per unit length on each of the wires in \(4.76\times10^{-2}\) N". A force per unit length carries units of \(\text{N m}^{-1}\), not N, and the word should be "is". The value is used above as \(4.76\times10^{-2}\) N/m, which is what reproduces the book's own printed answer of 56.68 A.]

[Textbook misprint: the question does not supply the proton mass, which the calculation requires. The standard value \(m_p = 1.67\times10^{-27}\) kg — the value this book's own Q.17 supplies for the same particle — is used above, and it reproduces the printed answer.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key is \(B = \dfrac{J_0\mu_0 r}{3a}\), which is dimensionally impossible for a magnetic field — \((\text{T m A}^{-1})(\text{A m}^{-2})(\text{m})/(\text{m})\) reduces to \(\text{T m}^{-1}\), not T. Integrating the given \(J = J_0 r/a\) over the enclosed area gives \(I_{enclosed} = \dfrac{2\pi J_0 r^{3}}{3a}\) and hence \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 J_0 r^{2}}{3a}\); the printed key has lost the square on \(r\).]
